still legal tender) | frequently_used_banknotes = {{lang|bn|৳}}5, {{lang|bn|৳}}10, {{lang|bn|৳}}20, {{lang|bn|৳}}50, {{lang|bn|৳}}100, {{lang|bn|৳}}200, {{lang|bn|৳}}500 and {{lang|bn|৳}}1000 | rarely_used_banknotes = {{lang|bn|৳}}1, {{lang|bn|৳}}2 | printer = [[The Security Printing Corporation (Bangladesh) Ltd.|The Security Printing Corporation Bangladesh Ltd.]] | printer_website = {{URL|www.spcbl.org.bd}} | mint = [[The Security Printing Corporation (Bangladesh) Ltd.|The Security Printing Corporation Bangladesh Ltd.]] }} {{Contains special characters|Bengali}} The '''Bangladeshi taka''' ({{lang-bn|টাকা}}, [[currency sign|sign]]: '''{{lang|bn|৳}}''', [[ISO 4217|code]]: '''BDT''', [[Short form (linguistics)|short form]]: '''Tk''') is the currency of the [[Bangladesh|People's Republic of Bangladesh]]. In Unicode, it is encoded at {{unichar|09F3|html=}}. Issuance of bank notes {{lang|bn|৳}}10 and larger is controlled by [[Bangladesh Bank]], while the {{lang|bn|৳}}2 and {{lang|bn|৳}}5 banknotes are the responsibility of the [[Ministry of Finance (Bangladesh)|ministry of finance]] of the [[government of Bangladesh]]. The banknotes of Tk. 2 and Tk.5 have mostly been replaced by coins while lower denomination coins (including all poysha coins) up to Tk. 1 have almost gone out of circulation due to inflation. The most commonly used symbol for the taka is "{{lang|bn|৳}}" and "Tk", used on receipts while purchasing goods and services. It is divided into 100 [[paisa|poysha]], but poysha coins are no longer in circulation. The poysha is still used for accounting purposes (e.g., Tk 123,456.78 for 123,456 taka and 78 poysha). ==Etymology== [[File:Silver Coin of Jalaluddin.jpg|thumb| [[Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah|Jalaluddin]]'s tanka (taka), [[Bengal Sultanate]], 15th century ]] According to ''[[The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language]]'' and ''[[Banglapedia]]'', the word ''taka'' came from the [[Sanskrit]] word ''tankah''.{{cite encyclopedia |title=taka |encyclopedia=The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language |year=2022 |edition=5th |publisher=HarperCollins Publishers |url=https://www.ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=taka |access-date=25 February 2022}}{{Cite web |url=http://en.banglapedia.org/index.php?title=Taka |title=Taka |website=Banglapedia}} The word ''taka'' in [[Bengali language|Bangla]] is also commonly used generically to mean any money, currency, or notes. Thus, colloquially, a person speaking in Bangla may use "taka" to refer to money regardless of what currency it is denominated in. This is also common in the Indian states of [[West Bengal]] and [[Tripura]], where the official name of the [[Indian rupee]] is "taka" as well. In other eastern Indian languages with the influence of [[Prakrit]] in [[Bihar]] it is "taka" in [[Maithili language|Maithili]] and [[Magahi language|Magadhi]] languages, in [[Assam]] it is টকা ''tôka'' and it is ଟଙ୍କା ''taṅkā'' in [[Odisha]]. ==History== {{Further|History of the taka}} ===1947–71=== After the [[Partition of Bengal (1947)|Partition of Bengal in 1947]], [[East Bengal]] became the eastern wing of [[Dominion of Pakistan|Pakistan]] and was renamed to [[East Pakistan]] in 1956. The [[Pakistani rupee]] also bore the word taka on official notes and coins. [[Bengali language|Bangla]] was one of the two national languages of the Pakistan union between 1956 and 1971 (the other being Urdu). The Bangladeshi taka came into existence since 1972, a year after the independence of the eastern wing of the union, as the independent nation of [[Bangladesh]]. Prior to the [[Bangladesh Liberation war|Liberation war]] in 1971, banknotes of the [[State Bank of Pakistan]] circulated throughout Bangladesh, and continued to be used in Bangladesh even after independence for only about three months until the official introduction of the taka on 4 March 1972. During the war, it was an unofficial practice of some [[Bengali nationalism|Bengali nationalists]] to protest Pakistani rule by stamping banknotes with "{{lang|bn|বাংলা দেশ}}" and "BANGLA DESH" as two words in either Bangla or English. These locally produced stamps are known to exist in several varieties, as are forgeries. On 8 June 1971, the Pakistani government declared that all banknotes bearing such stamps ceased to be legal tender. Furthermore, to prevent looted high-denomination notes from disrupting the Pakistani economy, the government also withdrew the [[legal tender]] status of all 100- and 500-rupee notes.{{cite book |last1=Linzmayer |first1=Owen |title=The Banknote Book |chapter=Bangladesh |year=2012 |location=San Francisco, CA |url=http://www.banknotebook.com}} Some foreign publications mention that there were rubber stamp "BANGLA DESH" overprints on different denominations of Pakistani bank notes during the a.m. period{{Clarify|date=April 2017}}. Pakistani postage stamps were rubber-stamped and used all over Bangladesh until 30 March 1973, but [[Bangladesh Bank]] or the Ministry of Finance never issued an order to overprint or rubber-stamp [[Pakistani rupee|Pakistani currency]].{{cite web |url=http://www.banknote.ws/COLLECTION/countries/ASI/BDE/BDE.htm |title=Bangladesh |website=www.banknote.ws}} ===Since 1972=== The taka was introduced in Bangladesh in 1972, replacing the [[Pakistani rupee]] at par. ====Treasury banknotes==== * The first treasury notes in 1972 for {{lang|bn|৳}}1 and notes of the [[Bangladesh Bank]] for {{lang|bn|৳}}5, {{lang|bn|৳}}10 and {{lang|bn|৳}}100. * In 1977, banknotes for {{lang|bn|৳}}50 were introduced, followed by {{lang|bn|৳}}500 in 1979 and {{lang|bn|৳}}20 in 1982. * {{lang|bn|৳}}1 treasury notes were issued until 1992, with {{lang|bn|৳}}2 treasury notes introduced in 1989. * {{lang|bn|৳}}1000 banknotes were introduced in 2008. * {{lang|bn|৳}}5 banknotes, previously issued by [[Bangladesh Bank]], are now issued by the [[Government of Bangladesh]]. These have mostly been replaced by coins since the early 2000s. ====Banknotes and issues==== In 2000, the government issued polymer {{lang|bn|৳}}10 notes as an experiment (similar to the Australian dollar). They proved unpopular, however, and were withdrawn later. At present, the {{lang|bn|৳}}1 and {{lang|bn|৳}}5 notes have mostly been replaced with coins, and in 2008, the government issued {{lang|bn|৳}}1,000 notes. In 2011, Bangladesh Bank began issuing a new series of banknotes denominated in {{lang|bn|৳}}2, {{lang|bn|৳}}5, {{lang|bn|৳}}100, {{lang|bn|৳}}500, and {{lang|bn|৳}}1000. All are dated 2011 and feature a portrait and watermark of the Father of the Nation, [[Sheikh Mujibur Rahman|Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman]], along the National Martyr's Monument in Savar at center front.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/17fc6d132aefa8953adbc584b2fc6012-1646.php |title=Bangladesh new note family confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} From 2011, the Bangladesh Bank introduced new notes denominated in {{lang|bn|৳}}10, {{lang|bn|৳}}20, and {{lang|bn|৳}}50 on 7 March 2012. The notes bear the portrait of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the National Martyr's Monument in Savar on the front. On the back of the notes, the {{lang|bn|৳}}10 will picture the [[Baitul Mukarram]] mosque, the {{lang|bn|৳}}20 pictures the [[Sixty Dome Mosque|Shat Gombuj]] mosque in Bagherat, and the {{lang|bn|৳}}50 notes feature [[Zainul Abedin|Shilpacharjo Zainul Abedin's]] famous painting ''Ploughing''.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/cd92830c856dc2ee5a757cc8574736b7-1990.php |title=Bangladesh new 10-, 20-, and 50-taka notes confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} On March 7 of 2019, Bangladesh Bank released new ৳100 notes, which had the same design as 2011 Version, but had better security, a stronger Blue and were made of a different material. On December 15 of 2019, Bangladesh Bank issued new ৳50 banknotes, with the same design as the 2011 version, but had a different colour (orange, brown and fluorescent yellow-green), and a slightly different design in some parts. On March 17 of 2020, Bangladesh Bank introduced new ৳200 notes. They bear a portrait of [[Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman]] on both sides and a landscape picture of a village, river and boats. ====Commemorative banknotes==== In 2011, Bangladesh Bank also introduced a {{lang|bn|৳}}40 note to commemorate the "40th Victory Anniversary of Bangladesh". The commemorative note features a portrait of the Father of the Nation, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the National Martyr's Monument in Savar on front, and six armed men on back. Curiously, this note has an [[electrotype]] 10 in the watermark, indicating it was likely printed on extra {{lang|bn|৳}}10 banknote paper.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/0ec11f5c0f3ad65ff21d3d25484a80a2-1891.php |title=Bangladesh new 40-taka commemorative confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} On 15 February 2012, Bangladesh Bank has introduced a {{lang|bn|৳}}60 note to commemorate "60 years of National Movement". The commemorative note measures {{convert|130|x|60|mm}} and features the Shaeed Minar (Martyrs' monument) in Dhaka and five men on the back. Like the {{lang|bn|৳}}40 commemorative note, this note has an electrotype 50 in the watermark. It was likely printed on extra {{lang|bn|৳}}50 banknote paper.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/4961d7b587f32b87246045445af9b14b-1975.php |title=Bangladesh new 60-taka commemorative note confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} On 26 January 2013, Bangladesh Bank issued a {{lang|bn|৳}}25 note to commemorate the 25th anniversary (silver jubilee) of the Security Printing Corporation (Bangladesh) Ltd. On the front is the National Martyr's Monument in Savar, the designs of the previous series of the Bangladeshi taka notes and its postage stamps, three spotted deer and the magpie-robin (''[[doyel]]''). On the reverse is the headquarters of the Security Printing Corporation. Curiously, this note has an electrotype 10 in the watermark, indicating it was likely printed on extra {{lang|bn|৳}}10 banknote paper.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/d223cf0059cd21e1a1ce2022c92e780f-2442.php |title=Bangladesh new 25-taka commemorative note confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} On 8 July 2013, Bangladesh Bank issued a {{lang|bn|৳}}100 note to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the [[Bangladesh National Museum]]. The commemorative note features an 18th-century [[terracotta]] plaque of a horseman on the front and the Bangladesh National Museum on the back.{{cite web |url=http://banknotenews.com/files/a2abad8f48ac418cad55abb1aaf6df4c-2504.php |title=Bangladesh new 100-taka commemorative note confirmed |work=banknotenews.com}} ==Coins== [[File:50 and 25 paise coins from Bangladesh.jpg|thumb|50 poysha from 1984 (left) and 25 poysha from 1980 (right).]] In 1973, coins were introduced in denominations of 5, 10, 25 and [[Bangladeshi fifty-poysha coin|50 poysha]]. 1 poysha coins followed in 1974, with {{lang|bn|৳}}1 coins introduced in 1975. The 1, 5 and 10 poysha were struck in aluminium, with the 25 and 50 poysha struck in steel and the {{lang|bn|৳}}1 in copper-nickel. The 5 poysha were square with rounded corners, and the 10 poysha were scalloped. Steel {{lang|bn|৳}}5 were introduced in 1994, and a steel {{lang|bn|৳}}2 coin followed in 2004. 1 and 5 poysha coins are rarely found in circulation. The same is the case with the 10, 25, and 50 poysha coins, as they have lost value due to inflation over the years. Only the {{lang|bn|৳}}1, {{lang|bn|৳}}2 and {{lang|bn|৳}}5 are regularly found in circulation. Unlike most other countries, coins are not issued every year, the most recent coins, {{lang|bn|৳}}1, {{lang|bn|৳}}2 and {{lang|bn|৳}}5, were issued in 2013, 10 years ago. {|class="wikitable" style="font-size: 90%" !colspan="5"|1973 Series |- !rowspan="2"|Value !! rowspan="2"| Composition !!colspan="2"|Description !! rowspan="2"|first mint |- ! National Martyrs’ Monument in Savar; logo for the golden jubilee of independence | Freedom Fighters of the [[Mukti Bahini|Liberation Army]] | 2021 | | | Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on a pixelated background, electrotype 50 and bank logo |- |} == Exchange rates == === {{anchor|Historical exchange rates}}Historic exchange rates === Upon [[Independence of Bangladesh|Bangladesh's independence]], the value of the Bangladeshi taka was set between ৳7.5 and ৳8.0 to US$1. Except for fiscal year 1978, the taka's value relative to the US dollar declined every year from 1971 through the end of 1987. To help offset this phenomenon, Bangladesh first used the compensatory financing facility of the [[International Monetary Fund]] in fiscal year 1974. Despite the increasing need for assistance, the Mujib government was initially unwilling to meet the IMF's conditions on monetary and fiscal policy. By fiscal year 1975, however, the government revised its stance, declaring a [[devaluation]] of the taka by 56 percent and agreeing to establishing the Bangladesh Aid Group by the World Bank.{{cite book |last1=Lesser |first1=Lawrence B. |date=1989 |chapter=Money and Banking |chapter-url=http://countrystudies.us/bangladesh/61.htm |editor1-last=Heitzman |editor1-first=James |editor2-last=Worden |editor2-first=Robert |title=Bangladesh: A Country Study |url=http://countrystudies.us/bangladesh/ |location=Washington, D.C. |publisher=Federal Research Division, Library of Congress |pages=108–109}} Between 1980 and 1983, the taka sustained a decline of some 50 percent because of a deterioration in Bangladesh's [[balance of payments]]. Between 1985 and 1987, the taka was adjusted in frequent incremental steps, stabilising again around 12 percent lower in real terms against the US dollar, but at the same time narrowing the difference between the official rate and the preferential secondary rate from 15 percent to 7.5 percent. Accompanying this [[structural adjustment]] was an expansion in trade conducted at the secondary rate, to 53 percent of total exports and 28 percent of total imports. In mid-1987, the official rate was relatively stable, approaching less than ৳31 to US$1. In January 2011, US$1 was equivalent to approximately ৳72,{{cite web |title=Historical Exchange Rates |website=OANDA |access-date=3 January 2011 |url=http://www.oanda.com/currency/historical-rates |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110202154335/http://www.oanda.com/currency/historical-rates |archive-date=2 February 2011 |url-status=live}} as of 21 April 2012, US$1 was worth close to ৳82, and as of 9 September 2015 US$1 valued ৳77. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:left; margin:1em auto 1em auto;" |+ Bangladeshi taka per currency unit averaged over the year (January of every year) !
